title: Polo: Required Work
definition: Required labor service under colonial authority.
content:
Polo y servicios was a system of required labor during Spanish colonial rule. An authority could call on people to carry out work. Required service is different from choosing to volunteer. To explain a case, ask who ordered the work, who had to do it, where it took place and which rules applied then. Rules, exemptions and actual practice should not be treated as identical throughout the whole colonial period.

A fictional source card orders workers to report for a project. It tells us about a demand for labor. It does not prove that every worker agreed or that every person named actually arrived. We are studying how authority affected people. This is not a classroom work order: students will not assign forced work to classmates or earn rewards for doing so. Read the instruction, then ask what evidence would show the work actually carried out.

clues: The demand
Polo concerned required labor service, not simply a freely chosen gift.
The setting
Ask who was called, where and under which dated rules.
Action needs evidence
An order alone does not prove attendance, agreement or completed work.
task: A colonial order requires workers to report. Which idea fits?
It records a labor demand; attendance and agreement need more evidence
It proves every worker volunteered
It proves all work was finished
It is a produce-delivery receipt
reason: It records a labor demand; attendance and agreement need more evidence. An order alone does not prove attendance, agreement or completed work.

title: Time Away Had Consequences
definition: Time used for one task that cannot also be used for another.
content:
Required labor could take time away from household work and other needs. Travel could add to the time spent on a task. The effect depended on the work, distance, season and support available at home. We should investigate those conditions rather than assume that every household experienced the same burden. A project could serve colonial aims while placing demands on the people who worked on it.

Try a fictional schedule model. A household has six task slots. If two are assigned to travel and required work, four remain for other tasks. The slots are not historical days or a universal legal requirement. They show that time used in one place is unavailable for another task at the same moment. Compare the model with evidence about an actual case before describing what families lost or how they responded. Do not ask classmates to disclose private family problems.

Open the three clues and choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help. If this topic needs review, revisit its lesson before targeted practice.
clues: Time
Required work and travel could take time from other tasks.
Conditions
Distance, season and household support can change the burden.
Model limit
Six task slots illustrate a relationship, not a historical labor quota.
task: What does the six-slot model illustrate?
Required work can reduce time available for other tasks
Every worker served exactly six historical days
All households had identical burdens
Travel never takes time
reason: Required work can reduce time available for other tasks. Six task slots illustrate a relationship, not a historical labor quota.

title: Bandala: Compulsory Produce Delivery
definition: A colonial system of compulsory sale or delivery of agricultural products to the government.
content:
Bandala concerned agricultural products that people were required to supply to the colonial government. It is often described as a forced sale. The word sale must not make us assume the producer freely chose the transaction. A requirement to deliver produce is different from a requirement to provide labor, even though one household could face more than one kind of demand.

Imagine two fictional records. One calls workers to a project. The other orders a delivery of rice. Classify the demand first: labor service or produce delivery. Then ask how it was carried out. A delivery order does not establish that every producer delivered, that a promised price was paid, or that the transaction was fair. We use a labelled teaching bundle rather than an authentic delivery document or a universal quota. The details need a particular place and period.

Open the three clues and choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help. If this topic needs review, revisit its lesson before targeted practice.
clues: The product
Bandala required agricultural produce for the colonial government.
Choice matters
A compulsory sale is not the same as a freely chosen market sale.
Compare demands
Polo concerned labor; bandala concerned produce delivery.
task: One record calls workers and another requires rice delivery. How should they be distinguished?
Labor service and compulsory produce delivery are different demands
Both are necessarily voluntary gifts
Both prove that payment arrived
Both describe only classroom rewards
reason: Labor service and compulsory produce delivery are different demands. Polo concerned labor; bandala concerned produce delivery.

title: A Promise Is Not a Payment
definition: Evidence describing money or other agreed payment actually received.
content:
When investigating compulsory produce delivery, separate the demand, the delivery and the payment. A promise to pay is not the same as payment received. A delivery receipt can show goods were handed over without proving that the producer received the promised money. A complaint may report a problem, but the final outcome needs follow-up evidence.

Our fictional evidence desk contains a rice order, a delivery note and a promise of later payment. Together they support an account of what was demanded and recorded as delivered. They do not establish that the promise was fulfilled. Ask for an appropriate payment record and compare dates and amounts for the same transaction. Do not invent a price or assume that every bandala transaction ended in the same way. Learning points reward a supported explanation, not taking produce from other people.

Open the three clues and choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help. If this topic needs review, revisit its lesson before targeted practice.
clues: Demand
An order identifies what was required.
Delivery
A receipt can record goods handed over.
Payment
A promise of future payment does not prove payment was received.
task: A delivery note and a promise to pay are supplied. What remains to check?
Whether payment was actually received
Nothing, since a promise proves payment
Whether every producer volunteered
Whether a receipt shows every private belief
reason: Whether payment was actually received. A promise of future payment does not prove payment was received.

title: A Named Response: Sumuroy in Samar
definition: An action expressing opposition to a demand or treatment.
content:
The NHCP registry identifies Agustin Sumuroy with Palapag, Samar, and an uprising beginning on 1 June 1649 against forced labor and abuses. This gives us a named case of opposition to colonial demands. It does not mean every worker everywhere responded in the same way. Keep a leader, location, period and stated issue connected in your explanation.

The NCCA CulturEd account connects the workers problem with being compelled to go to Cavite for shipbuilding. Distance matters here: a demand could involve leaving the home area. We do not need to invent speeches or act out fighting to understand why the demand mattered. Our source guide is a modern learning aid, not a diary written by a worker. Explain the connection between labor, distance and protest, and identify what these short accounts do not tell us about each persons experience.

clues: A named case
The NHCP marker connects Sumuroy and Palapag with protest against forced labor and abuses in 1649.
Distance

Scope

A named protest against forced labor and abuses in a particular setting
Every worker had an identical response
All details of every workers life are known
Fighting earns extra learning points
reason: A named protest against forced labor and abuses in a particular setting. A named uprising does not establish every workers response or private motive.

title: Prepare Your Labor and Produce Report
definition: A colonial system of compulsory sale or delivery of agricultural products to the government.
content: Review the five ideas from this mission. Polo concerned required labor service. Time and travel could affect other household tasks. Bandala concerned compulsory produce delivery. A demand, a delivery and a payment promise are different stages. Sumuroys case shows a named response to forced labor and abuses. Imagine a fictional museum desk with a work order, a rice-delivery note and a payment promise. Classify each one, explain what it supports and say what still needs checking. Do not call forced work volunteering or treat a promise as money already received. The six-slot schedule is a model, not a legal quota. Keep actual claims tied to their place and period. The main quiz has five questions and three correct passes. If you need help, the review path leads back to learning content before targeted practice and a retry. Completing this mission gives its reward once; it does not complete Chapter 9. Complete all missions, then pass the chapter challenge to earn the chapter badge.
clues: The product
Bandala required agricultural produce for the colonial government.
Choice matters
A compulsory sale is not the same as a freely chosen market sale.
Compare demands
Polo concerned labor; bandala concerned produce delivery.
task: Which report best uses these lesson clues?
Separate labor, produce delivery and payment, using evidence for each stage
Call all demands voluntary gifts
Treat a payment promise as a receipt
Use six model slots as a universal legal quota
reason: Distinguish the kind of demand and use evidence for its actual effects and outcomes.
